Design QA · Live capture

Does the passport console read enterprise-grade?

Six full-page captures of the running app (Playwright, 1440px viewport), taken straight off localhost:8000 after the dark-console redesign — not mockups.

Subject FEOC Compliance Passport Build post-redesign, dark palette Method headless Chromium, real seed data
Yes, mostly

The screens carrying real weight — the dashboard, the review workflow, the passport certificate — hold up under real density and genuinely read like a product a defense buyer would trust. The three single-purpose screens (login, scan, keys) are clean but visibly unfinished in one specific way. Details below, screen by screen.

Holds up

  • Consistent dark palette + accent across every page, no drift
  • Status semantics (pass / fail / insufficient / blocking) stay legible even in dense tables
  • The review workflow survives real information density — flags, corrections, and a sub-lot table on one screen without turning to noise
  • The passport view's chain-of-custody tree and signature block read like something worth handing to an auditor

Gaps

  • Login / Scan / Signing key: content sits top-left in a mostly empty dark viewport — reads unfinished, not minimal
  • Document list has no search or pagination — fine at 12 rows, won't hold at real supplier volume
  • "Compile" as a button label is implementation language, not buyer language
  • Audit trail lists every raw page-view forever — will get noisy fast on a heavily-scanned part

Fig. 01 — Login

Branded header lands well; the page below it doesn't

Gap

The badge + wordmark + subtitle in the header is doing real work — it's the one piece of brand identity every other page inherits. But the card itself sits pinned to the top of a 1000px-tall viewport with nothing below it. On a real monitor that's a wall of empty black under a login form, which reads as an unstyled placeholder rather than a deliberate minimal layout.

Fix — vertically center the card (flex column, centered, min-height: 100vh on main), or give the empty half a quiet visual anchor. Same fix applies to Scan and Signing key below.

Fig. 02 — Review queue dashboard

The screen this redesign was actually for

Holds up

Stat strip, real drop zone, workflow summary, and material-type cards with progress bars — this is the closest thing in the app to the reference screenshots, and it earns the comparison. The document list's repeated filenames are seed/demo data, not a rendering bug, but they do expose the real gap: no search or filter once a design partner has uploaded a few hundred certificates instead of twelve.

Fig. 03 — Heat review workflow

The functional core, under real density

Holds up

This is the screen doing the most work in the entire app — open flags, a correction panel, a live sub-lot table, segregation attestation — and it stays legible. The red-bordered "needs attention" zone and the flagged sub-lot row read as urgent without turning into a wall of alert boxes. This is the strongest evidence the dark palette wasn't just a coat of paint; it survives the page that actually has something to say.

Fig. 04 — Digital Passport

The artifact a contracting officer actually sees

Holds up

Large verdict word, mono signature block, a chain-of-custody tree with real connector lines, a UII Data Matrix panel — this reads like a real compliance artifact, not a debug view. Two small notes: "Compile" as the lookup button's label is developer vocabulary leaking into buyer-facing copy ("Look up" or "Verify" says the same thing in their language); and the audit trail below lists every single "passport_viewed" event indefinitely, which will scroll for pages once a part gets scanned regularly on a production line.

Fig. 05 — Scan

Clean, single-purpose — same empty-viewport gap

Gap

The copy here is doing good, specific work ("the photo is never uploaded or sent anywhere") — exactly the kind of trust-building language a floor worker scanning a part needs. Same dead-space issue as login: one card near the top, nothing anchoring the rest of the screen.

Fig. 06 — Signing key

Correct, unglamorous, and unfinished in the same way

Gap

The two-panel split (current key status / generate a new one) is the right structure for a page most people visit once. Same empty-viewport issue as the other single-card pages.

Captured locally via Playwright + Chromium against the running dev server — no data leaves this machine.
